o: While any two equal characters sit within distance k, merge the right one into the left, always choosing the pair with the smallest left index (ties: smallest right index), one merge at a time. With |s| <= 100 we can afford full re-simulation after each deletion.
k: After each merge the string shrinks and distances shrink, so new close pairs can appear; simply restart the scan after every deletion.
The specified tie-breaking is just 'first pair found scanning i ascending, then j ascending'.

a.i: Loop: scan i from left; for each i scan j from i+1 to i+k; the first equal pair found is exactly the required (smallest left, then smallest right) pair. Delete s[j] and repeat. Terminate when a full scan finds nothing.
s: For i in order, for j in (i, i+k]: if s[j] == s[i], delete s[j] and restart.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case — up to n merges, each with an O(n*k) scan; trivial for n <= 100

w: Constraints are tiny, so clarity beats cleverness. Pitfall: checking closeness against stale indices — always recompute on the current string. A linked-list of last-seen positions per letter gives O(n*k) if constraints grew. Follow-up: count merges performed, or handle k = 0 (no merges ever).
